Rough path

Words: 1k Articles: 20
Analysis OurBigBook.com
A rough path augments a path with compatible higher-order iterated-integral data. The extra data records effects, such as signed area, that are not continuously determined by the first-level path in the uniform topology. A rough differential equation uses this enhancement to recover a continuous solution map for irregular drivers.

Control function for rough paths (ω(s,u)+ω(u,t)≤ω(s,t))

Words: 53
Rough path OurBigBook.com
A control is a continuous nonnegative function on ordered pairs of times, zero on the diagonal and superadditive as displayed. It measures the size of increments of a rough path, typically through ∣Xs,t(k)​∣≤ω(s,t)k/p. Continuous finite variation gives suitable controls, which let local estimates be stated without tying them to a particular time parametrization.

Rough differential equation (dY=V(Y)dX)

Words: 255 Articles: 3
Rough path OurBigBook.com
A rough differential equation interprets a differential equation using the higher-order data of its driving rough path. For 2<p<3, its local expansion includes Vi​(Ys​)Xs,ti​+DVj​(Ys​)Vi​(Ys​)Xs,tij​, with a remainder controlled at order greater than one. For a smooth driver it is the usual controlled ordinary differential equation; for enhanced Brownian motion it is the corresponding Stratonovich equation.

Pathlevel solution of a rough differential equation (yt​−ys​=∑1≤∣I∣≤⌊p⌋​(VI​id)(ys​)Xs,tI​+O(ω(s,t)θ))

Words: 68
Rough differential equation OurBigBook.com
A pathlevel solution is the ordinary state path satisfying a local rough Taylor expansion with a remainder of order θ>1 in a control function for rough paths. It specifies the first level of the solution, rather than requiring the full lifted solution as part of the definition. With vector fields of regularity Lipγ, γ>p, the Davie lemma bounds discrete Euler errors uniformly; compactness and passage to the limit give such a path.

Davie discrete sewing lemma (as,t​≤Cω(s,t)θ,θ>1)

Words: 73
Rough differential equation OurBigBook.com
For a finite time grid, suppose a nonnegative error is zero on neighboring points and obeys as,t​≤as,u​+au,t​+Lω(s,t)1/pas,u​+Aω(s,t)θ. For a control function for rough paths and θ>1, sufficiently small control intervals have the displayed bound with constants independent of the grid. Splitting near half the control size makes the higher-order errors contract, and handles a crossing single grid interval by its zero error. Applying this to local Euler composition errors yields compactness of approximate pathlevel solutions.

Universal limit theorem

Words: 62
Rough differential equation OurBigBook.com
For sufficiently regular vector fields, for example bounded fields with bounded derivatives through order three when 2<p<3, the solution map of a rough differential equation exists uniquely and is locally continuous in the rough path metric. Ordinary differential equations driven by smooth approximations therefore converge whenever their enhanced drivers converge. The theorem makes the enhancement, rather than just the original path, the correct input for a continuous solution map.

Enhanced Brownian motion (Bs,t​=(1,Bt​−Bs​,∫st​(Br​−Bs​)⊗∘dBr​))

Words: 285 Articles: 4
Rough path OurBigBook.com
The Stratonovich enhancement of Brownian motion is a geometric p-rough path for every p>2. Its second level consists of Lévy area and the prescribed symmetric tensor. Its increments satisfy the Chen identity and have finite Hölder rough-path norms at every exponent below 1/2.

Brownian rough path small-ball positivity (P(dp​(B,e)<ε)>0)

Words: 38
Enhanced Brownian motion OurBigBook.com
For every 2<p<3 and every positive radius, the canonical Brownian enhancement has positive probability of lying in the displayed rough path metric ball. This controls both displacement and area. Together with Cameron-Martin quasi-invariance of enhanced Brownian motion, it puts every lifted Cameron-Martin control in the support of enhanced Brownian motion.

Support of enhanced Brownian motion (suppL(B)={S2​(h):h∈H01​}​dp​)

Words: 68
Enhanced Brownian motion OurBigBook.com
For 2<p<3, the support of a measure of enhanced Brownian motion is the rough-path closure of path signatures of paths in the Cameron-Martin space of Wiener measure. Polygonal convergence gives one inclusion. For the reverse inclusion, decompose Brownian motion into its polygonal interpolation and independent pinned bridges. The bridge enhancement becomes small in probability as the mesh decreases, while every finite-dimensional neighborhood of the polygonal vertices has positive Gaussian probability. Rough path translation then gives positive probability in every ball around a prescribed control path signature.

Nested polygonal approximation of Brownian rough paths

Words: 139 Articles: 1
Enhanced Brownian motion OurBigBook.com
For deterministic nested partitions with mesh tending to zero, lift the polygonal interpolation of Brownian motion by its ordinary iterated integrals. These path signatures converge almost surely to enhanced Brownian motion in every Hölder rough-path metric of exponent below 1/2, hence in p-variation for p>2. Conditioning on the partition values gives a nested martingale for the first level and the off-diagonal second levels. Moment bounds and interpolation upgrade pointwise convergence to convergence in the rough path metric.
Brownian rough path martingale Hölder bound (∥S2​(B(n))∥α​≤CE[∥B∥α2​∣Fn​]​)
Words: 69
Nested polygonal approximation of Brownian rough paths OurBigBook.com
Condition on the Brownian values at a dyadic mesh. First-level increments and antisymmetric area increments of its polygonal lift are conditional expectations of the corresponding Brownian increments. Conditional Jensen inequalities and the homogeneous degree-two norm give the displayed bound. The Doob maximal inequality makes the right-hand side uniformly finite almost surely when the Brownian Hölder norm has sufficiently many moments. Dense-time martingale convergence and equicontinuity then yield simultaneous convergence at every time.

Signature of a bounded variation path (SN​(x)s,t​=(1,∫st​dx,…,∫s<u1​<⋯<uN​<t​dxu1​​⊗⋯⊗dxuN​​))

Words: 169 Articles: 3
Rough path OurBigBook.com
The path signature collects the ordered iterated Riemann-Stieltjes integrals of a continuous path of bounded variation. Its truncation belongs to the free step-N nilpotent Lie group. It multiplies under concatenation by the Chen identity, is independent of orientation-preserving reparametrisation of the whole path, and records more than its endpoint displacement.

Iterated integral of a path (∫s<u1​<⋯<uk​<t​dxu1​​⊗⋯⊗dxuk​​)

Words: 88 Articles: 1
Signature of a bounded variation path OurBigBook.com
For a continuous path of bounded variation, integrate successively over the ordered simplex using Riemann-Stieltjes integrals. These integrals form the levels of its path signature. Appending the final integration variable gives the differential recursion dSt(k)​=St(k−1)​⊗dxt​.
Shuffle identity for iterated integrals
Words: 54
Iterated integral of a path OurBigBook.com
The product of two coordinate iterated integrals of a path is the sum over order-preserving interleavings of their integration variables. Split the product of the two ordered simplices according to the joint order of all variables. This identity explains the algebraic constraints on a geometric rough path and the cancellation of low-degree terms in the composition of its local Euler maps.

Chen identity (SN​(x)s,u​=SN​(x)s,t​⊗SN​(x)t,u​)

Words: 41
Signature of a bounded variation path OurBigBook.com
Partition each ordered integration simplex according to the number of times before the concatenation point. The integral over each resulting region factors into an initial iterated integral and a final iterated integral. Summing these factorizations proves the identity in the truncated tensor algebra.

Rough path metric (dp​(X,Y)=max1≤k≤⌊p⌋​(supD​∑[u,v]∈D​∣Xu,v(k)​−Yu,v(k)​∣p/k)k/p)

Words: 45
Rough path OurBigBook.com
This inhomogeneous variation metric compares the tensor increments level by level. A common alternative is the Hölder metric ρα​=maxk​sups<t​∣Xs,t(k)​−Ys,t(k)​∣/∣t−s∣kα. On a finite interval convergence in this metric implies p-variation convergence whenever pα≥1. Both topologies control the iterated integrals needed by the universal limit theorem.

Geometric p-rough path

Words: 176 Articles: 2
Rough path OurBigBook.com
A geometric p-rough path is a limit, in the rough path metric, of path signatures of sufficiently regular paths. It is a weak geometric p-rough path. At the same exponent these definitions need not coincide; weak geometric paths can be approximated after slightly weakening the variation exponent. The Brownian enhancement is geometric for every p>2.

Rough path translation (Th​X)

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Geometric p-rough path OurBigBook.com
For 2<p<3 and a continuous path h of bounded variation, translate the first level by h and add the mixed integrals ∫Xs,r​⊗dhr​, ∫hs,r​⊗dXr​ and ∫hs,r​⊗dhr​ to the second level. Integration by parts defines the second mixed integral. The operation is continuous in the rough path metric and the variation norm of h. For canonical lifts it is precisely the enhancement of the sum of the paths.
Cameron-Martin quasi-invariance of enhanced Brownian motion
Words: 59
Rough path translation OurBigBook.com
For a deterministic path h in the Cameron-Martin space of Wiener measure, the law of Th​B is equivalent to the law of enhanced Brownian motion. The Cameron-Martin theorem gives equivalence for the underlying Brownian paths; the canonical enhancement of the translated path is exactly the rough-path translation, including its mixed area terms. Continuity of this translation transfers small-ball positivity at the identity to every control signature.

Weak geometric p-rough path (X:[0,T]→G⌊p⌋(Rd))

Words: 106 Articles: 1
Rough path OurBigBook.com
A weak geometric p-rough path is a continuous path in the free step-N nilpotent Lie group, with N=⌊p⌋, whose increments have finite p-variation for the Carnot-Carathéodory distance. Its multiplicative increments are Xs,t​=Xs−1​⊗Xt​. They obey the Chen identity and the algebraic symmetries of path signatures.

Pure-area rough path (yt​=exp(t[e1​,e2​]))

Words: 62
Weak geometric p-rough path OurBigBook.com
The first level of this group path is zero but its second level grows linearly. Its Carnot-Carathéodory distance increments are a constant times ∣t−s∣1/2. It therefore has finite p-variation precisely when p≥2, and is a step-two weak geometric rough path at p=2, even though its first-level trace is constant. For higher truncations the same Lie exponential defines a compatible lift.

Potential theory

Words: 76 Articles: 1
Analysis OurBigBook.com
Potential theory studies harmonic functions, subharmonic functions, and the Laplace operator, including harmonic measure, regular boundary points, and the Dirichlet problem. The Brownian representation of the Dirichlet problem connects these analytic objects with exit probability distributions.

Dirichlet form (E)

Words: 56
Potential theory OurBigBook.com
A Dirichlet form on a real L2 space is a densely defined closed nonnegative symmetric bilinear form with the Markov contraction property. In the real case, truncating u to (0∨u)∧1 keeps it in the form domain and cannot increase E(u,u). The Dirichlet form of a Markov chain is a discrete energy example; Laplacian energy on a region supplies a continuous example.

Integral equation

Words: 634 Articles: 12
Analysis OurBigBook.com
An integral equation asks for an unknown function that occurs under an integral. Integral equations with a variable upper limit have a triangular dependence structure that often permits successive approximation.

Abel integral equation (g(x)=∫xb​f(y)(y−x)−1/2dy)

Words: 213 Articles: 2
Integral equation OurBigBook.com
This square-root-kernel integral equation is inverted by integrating g(x)/x−z​ over z<x<b and interchanging integrations. The inner integral over z<x<y equals π, so ∫zb​g(x)/x−z​dx=π∫zb​f(y)dy. Differentiating recovers f(z)=−π−1d[∫zb​g(x)/x−z​dx]/dz. The changes of variables x=p2, y=η2 put the angular-ray equation into this form.

Derivative of an Abel integral (dxd​∫0x​x−t​h(t)​dt=x​h(0)​+∫0x​x−t​h′(t)​dt)

Words: 90
Abel integral equation OurBigBook.com
Suppose h is continuously differentiable on [0,L]. For 0<x≤L, the improper integral g(x)=∫0x​h(t)(x−t)−1/2dt exists, but substituting directly into the ordinary Leibniz integral rule produces an undefined endpoint term. First use integration by parts to obtain
g(x)=2h(0)x​+2∫0x​h′(t)x−t​dt.
(1)
The new endpoint term at t=x vanishes, and the differentiated kernel is locally integrable. Differentiating gives the displayed formula. One rigorous justification rewrites the second term as ∫0x​[∫0s​h′(t)(s−t)−1/2dt]ds by Fubini's theorem; the inner integral is continuous for s>0, so the fundamental theorem of calculus applies. Moreover g(x)=2h(0)x​+O(x3/2): if h(0)=0, the right difference quotient at zero diverges rather than defining a finite derivative.

Abel integral equation of fractional order (∫0t​Φ(τ)(t−τ)−αdτ=f(t),0<α<1)

Words: 82
Abel integral equation OurBigBook.com
For an absolutely continuous f with f(0)=0, this causal Abel integral equation has inversion
Φ(t)=Γ(α)Γ(1−α)1​∫0t​f′(τ)(t−τ)α−1dτ.
(2)
Under Laplace-transform growth hypotheses, the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms converts the original kernel into Γ(1−α)sα−1. Since L[f′]=sL[f], the transformed inverse is s−αL[f′]/Γ(1−α), giving the formula. It also holds locally in the corresponding integrable convolution class: convolving the two power kernels produces the constant B(α,1−α)=Γ(α)Γ(1−α) by the beta-gamma identity, so substitution recovers ∫0t​f′=f(t). The same convolution identity proves uniqueness in that class. For example f(t)=t gives Φ=tα/[Γ(α+1)Γ(1−α)].

Linear integral equation ((I+K)f=g)

Words: 50
Integral equation OurBigBook.com
A linear integral equation depends linearly on its unknown function. For example, (I+K)f=g with (Kf)(x)=∫K(x,y)f(y)dy has a trivial homogeneous null space whenever its inhomogeneous problem has a unique solution: otherwise a nonzero homogeneous solution could be added to that solution. This is the uniqueness step used in dressing constructions of a Lax pair.

Volterra integral equation

Words: 341 Articles: 7
Integral equation OurBigBook.com
A Volterra integral equation has a variable integration limit, so its value at a point depends only on earlier values. Repeated integration produces factorial decay, which often makes its Neumann series converge without a smallness assumption.

Laplace solution of a first-order equation with exponential memory (x′+e−2t∗x=1,x(0)=0)

Words: 53
Volterra integral equation OurBigBook.com
The derivative and convolution theorem for Laplace transforms give [p+1/(p+2)]xˉ=1/p. Partial fractions yield xˉ=2/p−2/(p+1)−1/(p+1)2, so x(t)=2−(2+t)e−t tends to two. A direct check gives x′=(1+t)e−t and (e−2t∗x)(t)=1−(1+t)e−t. Introducing the memory variable w=e−2t∗x gives the equivalent local system x′+w=1, w′=x−2w, w(0)=0, explaining why the transform denominator has a repeated pole at p=−1.

Sine-kernel Volterra resolvent (x+sin∗x=F⟹x=F−2​1​sin(2​⋅)∗F)

Volterra integral equation OurBigBook.com
For causal convolution on t≥0, the Laplace transform convolution theorem converts x+sin∗x=F into xˉ=[(p2+1)/(p2+2)]Fˉ. Since this multiplier is 1−1/(p2+2), inversion gives the displayed resolvent kernel. The formula remains valid for locally integrable forcing on finite intervals: substitution and the Fubini theorem reduce verification to an identity between the two continuous sine kernels. Thus a global Laplace transform is a convenient derivation, rather than an essential growth restriction on every local forcing.

A function weighting the influence of past values in a history-dependent equation. In a Volterra integral equation its convolution with the history is causal: only earlier times appear. For an integrable kernel, κ(0)=∫0∞​κ(u)du measures its response to a constant input. In a generalized Langevin equation, the friction memory kernel records delayed resistance to the velocity.

It is associative under the usual absolute-integrability hypotheses. The integration simplex gives factorial bounds for iterated convolutions of bounded kernels.

Power law (f(x)=Cxp)

Words: 570 Articles: 3
Analysis OurBigBook.com
A power law is a relation f(x)=Cxp, with fixed constants C and p. For positive x, any real number p is allowed. Its useful feature is a simple scaling rule:
f(λx)=λpf(x)(λ>0).
(5)
The same proportional change of input produces the same proportional change of output, independently of the starting value. The exponent controls that response; the coefficient fixes the magnitude.
For example, the area of a circle is A(r)=πr2. Doubling the radius multiplies its area by four, and tripling it multiplies the area by nine. The volume of a sphere is V(r)=4πr3/3: the same changes multiply its volume by eight and twenty-seven. The distinction explains why similarly shaped objects do not preserve their ratio of surface area to volume when their size changes.
When the output is positive, a logarithm turns the power law into a straight-line relation. Using positive reference values x0​ and f0​=f(x0​),
f0​f(x)​=(x0​x​)p,logf0​f(x)​=plogx0​x​.
(6)
These ratios are dimensionless quantities, so the formula also applies to physical measurements with units. Plotting both ratios on a logarithmic scale gives a line of slope p. Changing a unit changes the numerical coefficient, while the exponent stays the same. Positive p describes increasing values; negative p describes decreasing values; p=0 gives a constant. The zero coefficient is a degenerate case with no useful logarithmic slope.
Exact scaling is stronger than regular variation. The function x2logx has a doubling ratio tending to four, but its logarithmic correction keeps growing. The diagram contrasts it with the exact power law x2.
A power law for a probability density and a power law for a tail probability have different exponents. For a Pareto distribution with α>0 and lower endpoint one,
P(X>x)=x−α,pX​(x)=αx−α−1(x>1).
(7)
The tail probability has exponent −α; differentiating it and changing sign gives the probability density exponent −α−1. Confusing them changes the interpretation of a fitted exponent. The normalizing coefficient and lower endpoint also matter: a decreasing power law is not automatically a valid probability density over the entire positive real line.
The appearance of a line over a finite logarithmic range is evidence to investigate, rather than a proof of an exact power law or its mechanism. In their study of power-law distributions, Clauset, Shalizi and Newman combine maximum likelihood estimation, goodness-of-fit tests and comparisons with alternative models; their abstract explains why ordinary least-squares fitting can give misleading results for tail data. See Aaron Clauset, Cosma Rohilla Shalizi and M. E. J. Newman, Power-law distributions in empirical data, SIAM Review 51 (2009), 661–703. The scaling rule is mathematically exact when it defines a model; whether a dataset supports that model is a question of statistical inference.

Cauchy's functional equation (f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y))

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Functional equation OurBigBook.com
Cauchy's functional equation asks for functions f:R→R satisfying
f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)(x,y∈R).
(8)
The identity must hold for every pair of real numbers, and a solution is an additive function. It says that combining two inputs before applying f gives the same result as combining their outputs.[ref]
For example, f(x)=3x satisfies the identity because 3(x+y)=3x+3y. At x=2/3 and y=5/6 the two sides give
f(32​+65​)=f(23​)=29​,f(32​)+f(65​)=2+25​=29​.
(9)
For positive widths, a rectangle of height three makes this visible: cutting its width into x and y partitions its area into 3x and 3y. The same identity also holds for negative inputs, where 3x is a signed output rather than an ordinary area.
Every function f(x)=cx with a fixed real number c solves Cauchy's functional equation. The surprising question is whether these are all the solutions. Rational homogeneity of an additive function forces f(q)=qf(1) for every rational number q, but reaching an irrational number requires an additional argument. Continuity at just one point or being a bounded function on an interval of positive length supplies that argument; without such a condition, discontinuous additive functions exist.[ref]
This makes Cauchy's functional equation a useful test of the boundary between algebra and analysis: a rule about addition fixes all rational multiples, while a tiny amount of continuity fixes the entire real line. For example, the continuous exponential functional equation reduces to an additive function after taking a logarithm, so this result explains why its nonzero solutions are exponential functions.

An additive function on an additive semigroup satisfies f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y) whenever x, y, and x+y belong to its domain.
For real numbers, an additive function is a group homomorphism from (R,+) to itself. It preserves scalar multiplication by every rational number, so it is a linear map when domain and codomain are viewed as vector spaces over the rational numbers. Being a linear map over the real numbers additionally requires f(tx)=tf(x) for every real number t. On the real line this stronger condition is equivalent to f(x)=xf(1). Additivity alone does not imply it.

A saddle point of a differentiable real-valued function is a critical point which is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. For example f(x,y)=x2−y2 has a saddle at the origin. Critical point (∇f(x∗​)=0)

Words: 2k Articles: 20
Analysis OurBigBook.com
For a smooth function f:U→R on an open set U⊆Rn, a critical point is an input x∗​ where the gradient vanishes: ∇f(x∗​)=0. Equivalently, every first partial derivative is zero. Such a critical point is a stationary point; in one variable the condition is f′(x∗​)=0.
There is a broader convention in elementary one-variable calculus: a "critical number" is an interior input where the derivative is zero or does not exist, provided the function itself is defined there. Thus a corner can be a critical number without being a stationary point. Here the smooth meaning of critical point is used unless the broader convention is explicitly stated. [ref]
For the polynomial f(x)=x4−2x2 on the real line,
f′(x)=4x(x2−1),f′(−1)=f′(0)=f′(1)=0,f(−1)=f(1)=−1,f(0)=0.
(57)
The stationary points at x=±1 are strict local minima and attain the global minimum; the stationary point at x=0 is a strict local maximum. One can check the local classifications from f′′(x)=12x2−4, which is positive at ±1 and negative at zero. The identity f(x)=(x2−1)2−1≥−1 proves the global minimum directly. Since f(x)→+∞ as ∣x∣→∞, there is no global maximum on R.
A zero derivative alone does not guarantee an extremum. The polynomial g(x)=x3 has g′(0)=0 but is strictly increasing through zero: every neighbourhood of zero contains both positive and negative values, so zero is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum. Conversely, the absolute value function h(x)=∣x∣ has a strict local minimum and a unique global minimum at zero, but its left and right derivatives are −1 and +1. It is not differentiable there, so zero is a critical number under the broader convention and is not a stationary point.
The usefulness of critical points is that they reduce the search for smooth interior extrema to equations. Every local minimum or local maximum of a differentiable function at an interior point has zero gradient; this condition is necessary, and x3 shows that it is not sufficient. The striking feature is that all the first directional derivatives must vanish together, even though the surrounding values can form a valley, a peak, or a saddle point of a scalar function. [ref]
Proof outline: at an interior local minimum x∗​ in one variable, the difference quotient (f(x∗​+h)−f(x∗​))/h is nonnegative for small h>0 and nonpositive for small h<0. If the derivative exists, the two sides have the same limit, forcing f′(x∗​)=0. Reverse the inequalities for a local maximum. In several variables, apply this argument along each coordinate line to obtain zero partial derivatives and hence zero gradient. At a domain boundary, both directions may not be available: f(x)=x on [0,1] attains its global minimum at zero although f′(0)=1 for its smooth extension.

Words: 542 Articles: 3
Analysis OurBigBook.com
The residue of a function f at an isolated singularity a is its Laurent coefficient of degree −1. More explicitly, if f is holomorphic for 0<∣z−a∣<ρ, write its Laurent series as
f(z)=∑n=−∞∞​cn​(z−a)n,Res(f,a)=c−1​.
(127)
This one Laurent coefficient determines the contour integral around a sufficiently small counterclockwise circle about a. A complicated local Laurent series can therefore leave a remarkably simple answer after one complete trip around the point.
For a simple pole, multiplying by z−a removes the pole, leaving a holomorphic extension whose value at a is the residue:
Res(f,a)=limz→a​(z−a)f(z).
(128)
There is a useful shortcut for a quotient f=g/h. If g and h are holomorphic near a, h has a simple zero there, and g(a)=0, then f has a simple pole and
Res(g/h,a)=h′(a)g(a)​.
(129)
The first-order Taylor series of h explains the denominator: dividing h(z) by z−a leaves its derivative at a in the limit. This computes a residue without finding the full Laurent series, which is especially useful when the numerator or denominator is complicated. [ref]
For example, the rational function f(z)=1/(z2+1) has simple poles at i and −i. Factoring the denominator makes both residues immediately visible:
f(z)=(z−i)(z+i)1​,Res(f,i)=2i1​=−2i​,Res(f,−i)=−2i1​=2i​.
(130)
The signs matter: these residues cancel when both poles are enclosed, but either one contributes when enclosed alone. The residue theorem below turns this distinction into different contour integrals of the same function.
A residue is not the same thing as a pole, nor does it measure the order of a pole. The function 1/z2 has a double pole at zero but residue zero. Conversely,
e1/z=1+z1​+2!z21​+3!z31​+⋯
(131)
has an essential singularity at zero and residue one. Infinitely many negative powers cause no difficulty in reading off that particular Laurent coefficient. At a removable singularity the residue is zero. [ref]
Why does only this Laurent coefficient survive? Parametrize a counterclockwise circle by z=a+reit, 0≤t≤2π, with 0<r<ρ. For every integer n,

(132)
When n=−1, the complex exponential completes a whole number of turns and its contributions cancel; when n=−1, it is constant. Uniform convergence of the Laurent series on this circle justifies termwise integration, giving ∮f(z)dz=2πiRes(f,a). Thus the residue isolates exactly the local information that a closed contour integral detects. [ref]
This selection rule explains why a very large value near an isolated singularity need not produce a large contour integral. The double pole 1/z2 grows faster near zero than 1/z, yet its contributions around a circle cancel completely. What matters is the arrangement of complex values along the path, including the differential dz, rather than their moduli alone. A residue records that surviving contribution, not the size of the function near the point.

Residue theorem (∮Γ​f(z)dz=2πi∑j​Res(f,aj​))

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Analysis OurBigBook.com
Let Γ be a piecewise smooth contour forming a simple closed curve, positively oriented: travel counterclockwise, with the interior on the left. Suppose f is holomorphic on an open set containing Γ and its interior, except at finitely many isolated singularities a1​,…,am​ strictly inside. Then
∮Γ​f(z)dz=2πi∑j=1m​Res(f,aj​).
(135)
No isolated singularity may lie on Γ: the ordinary contour integral must be defined there. Reversing the direction of the contour reverses the sign of the answer. The theorem applies to essential singularities as well as poles. [ref]
Return to f(z)=1/(z2+1). A counterclockwise circle ∣z∣=2 encloses both simple poles, so
∮∣z∣=2​z2+1dz​=2πi(−2i​+2i​)=0.
(136)
Yet f is nonzero everywhere it is defined. A zero contour integral does not imply a zero function, or even absence of poles: the enclosed residues can cancel. By contrast, the counterclockwise circle ∣z−i∣=1/2 encloses only i, giving
∮∣z−i∣=1/2​z2+1dz​=2πi(−2i​)=π.
(137)
The picture compares these two selections. Changing the shape of a contour while keeping the same enclosed poles leaves the contour integral unchanged, provided the contour deformation stays where f is holomorphic.
This is the practical appeal of the residue theorem: local Laurent coefficients determine a global contour integral. For a rational function, a few simple pole computations can replace a long parametrized calculation. It also makes real improper integrals accessible by treating the real line as part of a closed contour in the complex plane.
To compute I=∫−∞∞​dx/(1+x2), take R>1 and travel along the real line from −R to R, then return along the upper semicircle AR​, parametrized by z=Reit for 0≤t≤π. This contour is positively oriented and encloses the simple pole i only; −i is outside. Hence
∫−RR​1+x2dx​+∫AR​​1+z2dz​=π.
(138)
The added arc must be controlled before taking a limit. On AR​, the reverse triangle inequality gives ∣z2+1∣≥R2−1, and the arc length is πR. The estimation lemma therefore yields
​∫AR​​1+z2dz​​≤R2−1πR​⟶0.
(139)
The denominator grows quadratically while the arc length grows only linearly. This quantitative comparison, rather than a sketch alone, explains why closing the contour does not alter the limiting real improper integral. It even supplies an error bound: the difference between π and the finite real integral is at most πR/(R2−1).
For a numerical check, R=10 gives the finite real integral 2arctan(10)≈2.94226, leaving about 0.19934 to reach π. The arc bound is 10π/99≈0.31733, comfortably larger than that error. The graph shows both quantities approaching zero. The exact tail here can be checked with the antiderivative arctanx; the residue theorem method remains useful for improper integrals where a convenient real antiderivative is unavailable.
Finally, both one-sided improper integrals converge absolutely: for ∣x∣≥1, 0<1/(1+x2)≤1/x2, whose tails are integrable. Thus the symmetric limit computes the ordinary improper integral, not merely a Cauchy principal value, and
∫−∞∞​1+x2dx​=π.
(140)
Closing below instead would enclose the simple pole −i. With the same left-to-right traversal of the real line, that contour is clockwise, so its contour integral is −2πiRes(f,−i)=π again. This provides a useful sign check: the opposite residue is accompanied by the opposite direction around the enclosed region.
The same strategy extends to many other rational functions: choose a contour, identify its enclosed isolated singularities, compute their residues, and bound the added pieces. The choice of contour and the bound are as much part of the calculation as the residues. [ref]

Optional stopping gives g(z)=Ez​g(ZTr​​), hence ∣g(z)∣≤1/r. Letting r increase to one proves the displayed bound.
If ∣g(z0​)∣=1 at a nonzero point, put c=g(z0​). The same expectation identity forces Re(cg(ZTr​​))=1 almost surely. The exit density is strictly positive on every boundary arc by the Poisson kernel for the unit disk, and g is continuous there, so g=c on that circle. The expectation identity for every starting point inside it then gives g=c throughout that smaller disk. Letting r increase to one shows f(z)=cz on the full disk, with ∣c∣=1. This derives both the inequality and its rigidity using Brownian harmonic measure.

Uniqueness of Poisson equation OurBigBook.com
The difference of two classical Poisson equation solutions with the same Dirichlet boundary conditions is a harmonic function vanishing on the boundary. Under sufficient boundary smoothness, Green's first identity gives ∫V​∣∇(ϕ1​−ϕ2​)∣2=0. More generally the maximum principle for harmonic functions proves the same uniqueness for functions continuous up to the boundary and twice continuously differentiable in the bounded interior.

Uniqueness for a harmonic transmission problem (k1​∫Ω1​​∣∇w∣2+k2​∫Ω2​​∣∇w∣2=0)

Words: 125
Dirichlet uniqueness for the Poisson equation OurBigBook.com
Let a bounded connected body consist of two regions with positive constant thermal conductivities k1​,k2​. A temperature is harmonic in each region, continuous across their interface, has continuous normal heat flux there, and has prescribed outer Dirichlet boundary conditions. There is at most one sufficiently regular solution.
For the difference w of two solutions, apply Green's first identity in each region and multiply by its thermal conductivity. The interface outward normals are opposite, so continuity of w and k∂n​w cancels their boundary terms. The outer term vanishes because w=0. Hence the displayed sum of nonnegative Dirichlet energies is zero. The gradient vanishes in both regions; continuity and the outer data then force w=0. The proof also applies to finitely many connected subregions, provided the union is connected and the same transmission conditions hold.

Analysis OurBigBook.com
A fixed-point theorem gives conditions under which a map T has a point satisfying Tx=x.

Schauder fixed-point theorem (T(K)⊂K⟹∃u∈K:T(u)=u)

Words: 397 Articles: 4
Fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
Every continuous map from a nonempty compact convex set K in a Banach space to itself has a fixed point. A useful equivalent form takes a nonempty closed bounded convex set C and a continuous map T:C→C whose image is relatively compact. To obtain this version from the compact-domain version, restrict T to convT(C)⊂C and use closed convex hull of a compact set.
For a proof on K, the Schauder approximation lemma gives continuous maps Tε​:K→K∩Lε​ with finite-dimensional Lε​ and ∥T−Tε​∥∞​≤ε. The Brouwer fixed-point theorem on the nonempty compact convex set K∩Lε​ gives xε​=Tε​xε​, so ∥Txε​−xε​∥≤ε. A convergent subsequence as ε↓0 and the continuity of T give an exact fixed point.

Schauder solution of a small Hammerstein integral equation (u(x)=μ∫01​G(x,y)f(y,u(y))dy)

Words: 68
Schauder fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
For continuous G and f, restrict to the closed supremum-norm ball of radius R in C([0,1]). Boundedness on the compact kernel and nonlinearity boxes makes the integral map preserve this ball for sufficiently small positive μ. Uniform continuity of f proves continuity of the map; uniform continuity of G gives an equicontinuous bounded image. Arzelà-Ascoli makes that image relatively compact, and Schauder gives a solution. No global Lipschitz hypothesis or uniqueness conclusion is needed.

Bounded semilinear Dirichlet existence theorem (−Δu=f(u),u∈H01​(Ω),f∈Cb​(R))

Words: 158 Articles: 1
Schauder fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
For a smooth bounded domain and a bounded continuous scalar function f, this problem has a weak solution. Let S be the zero-Dirichlet inverse of −Δ, defined by the Lax-Milgram theorem. The Poincaré inequality gives ∥Sh∥2​≤CP2​∥h∥2​. The Rellich-Kondrachov compactness theorem makes S:L2→L2 compact. The Nemytskii operator Nf​ is continuous and has bounded image, so T=S∘Nf​ is a nonlinear compact operator mapping a sufficiently large closed L2 ball into itself. The Schauder fixed-point theorem gives a fixed point, necessarily in H01​, and its defining identity is the desired weak formulation. This proves existence; uniqueness requires additional assumptions.
Nonnegative truncation of a semilinear source (F(s)=f(max{s,0}))
Words: 72
Bounded semilinear Dirichlet existence theorem OurBigBook.com
If f is continuous, bounded and nonnegative on [0,∞), extend it to a bounded continuous function on the real line by the displayed formula. The bounded semilinear Dirichlet existence theorem gives −Δu=F(u) with u∈H01​. Test with the negative part u−​=max{−u,0} to obtain −∥∇u−​∥22​=∫F(u)u−​≥0. The Poincaré inequality gives u−​=0, so u≥0 and F(u)=f(u). Thus singularities or uncontrolled growth of the original formula at negative arguments need not prevent a nonnegative weak solution.

Schauder approximation lemma (supx∈K​∥T(x)−Tε​(x)∥≤ε)

Words: 82
Schauder fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
Let K be a nonempty compact convex set in a Banach space and T:K→K a continuous map. For every ε>0, there is a finite-dimensional linear subspace Lε​ and a continuous map Tε​:K→K∩Lε​ that approximates T uniformly to within ε in norm.
Choose y1​,…,yN​∈T(K) whose open radius-ε balls cover the compact image T(K). Set wi​(x)=max{0,ε−∥Tx−yi​∥} and
Tε​(x)=∑i​wi​(x)∑i​wi​(x)yi​​.
(149)
The denominator is positive. This convex combination belongs to K∩span{y1​,…,yN​} and depends continuously on x. Every contributing yi​ has distance less than ε from Tx, so the triangle inequality gives ∥Tε​(x)−Tx∥<ε.

Strict distance decrease on a compact metric space (d(fx,fy)<d(x,y)(x=y))

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
A self-map f of a nonempty compact metric space satisfying the displayed strict distance inequality has exactly one fixed point, although a uniform contraction constant need not exist. The inequality makes f Lipschitz continuous with constant at most one, so g(x)=d(fx,x) is continuous and attains a minimum at p. If fp=p, then g(fp)<g(p), a contradiction. Two different fixed points contradict the same distance inequality.

Bounded-orbit fixed point for a strictly distance-decreasing Euclidean map

Words: 44
Strict distance decrease on a compact metric space OurBigBook.com
For a strictly distance-decreasing map of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, one bounded forward orbit suffices for existence of a fixed point. Its closure is compact by the Heine-Borel theorem and invariant by continuity, so strict distance decrease on a compact metric space applies. Strict distance decrease gives uniqueness throughout the whole space, not merely the orbit closure.

Kakutani fixed-point theorem

Words: 30
Fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
A nonempty compact convex set K in a finite-dimensional space and an upper hemicontinuous set-valued mapping F:K⇉K with nonempty closed convex values admit x∈F(x). A closed graph suffices when the whole output space is compact.

Words: 47
Fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
Every continuous self-map of a nonempty compact convex subset of a locally convex space has a fixed point. Compactness is in the locally convex topology, which may be weaker than a norm topology. This version permits fixed-point arguments on a weak-star topology compact set of linear functionals. See Hartman's fixed-point chapter, Theorem 0.2.

Leray-Schauder fixed point theorem

Words: 42
Fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
Let T be a compact continuous self-map of a Banach space. If the set of solutions of u=tT(u) for 0≤t≤1 is bounded, then T has a fixed point. The theorem converts a priori estimates for a homotopy of equations into existence.

Knaster-Tarski theorem

Words: 37
Fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
Every monotone self-map of a complete lattice has a complete lattice of fixed points. Its least fixed point is the meet of its prefixed points, and its greatest fixed point is the join of its postfixed points.

A topological space has the fixed-point property when every continuous self-map has a fixed point.

Fixed-point property OurBigBook.com
If h:A→B is a homeomorphism and A has the fixed-point property, then a continuous f:B→B induces h−1fh:A→A. A fixed point of the conjugate map is carried by h to a fixed point of f.

Fixed-point property OurBigBook.com
For continuous f:[0,1]→[0,1], the function f(x)−x is nonnegative at zero and nonpositive at one, so the intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point.

Contraction mapping theorem

Words: 1k Articles: 16
Fixed-point theorem OurBigBook.com
A contraction mapping T:X→X on a nonempty complete metric space has exactly one fixed point x∗​, and the sequence xn+1​=T(xn​) converges to x∗​ from every x0​∈X. The same constant 0≤L<1 must satisfy d(Tx,Ty)≤Ld(x,y) for all x,y∈X. The statement applies to metric spaces, including closed subsets of a Banach space; neither linearity nor a vector space structure is required.[ref]
The force of the result is that existence, uniqueness, and a practical approximation procedure arrive together. Repeated application produces corrections bounded by a geometric series, hence a Cauchy sequence; completeness supplies its limit. The Lipschitz continuity of T makes that limit a fixed point. Two different fixed points would have their positive distance multiplied by at most L<1 while remaining unchanged, which is impossible.

Uniform contraction from a comparison function on a bounded set (d(Tx,Ty)≤ψ(d(x,y))≤qd(x,y))

Words: 67
Contraction mapping theorem OurBigBook.com
Suppose all distances lie in [0,D], ψ is continuous, 0<ψ(r)<r for positive r, and limr→0​ψ(r)/r<1. The ratio is uniformly bounded below one near zero, and its maximum on the remaining compact scalar interval is also below one. Thus one constant q<1 works on the entire bounded set. If the set is complete and the map preserves it, Banach's theorem gives a unique fixed point. Compactness of the set itself is not required.

Semilinear Poisson contraction threshold (ϵCP2​<1)

Words: 77
Contraction mapping theorem OurBigBook.com
For a globally Lipschitz nonlinearity of constant ϵ, the map taking v to the zero-Dirichlet Poisson solution with load f(v) is a contraction in the gradient norm if the displayed inequality holds. Poincaré gives the factor CP​ from the Sobolev input to L2, and testing the linear Poisson equation gives another factor CP​ back to the gradient norm. The condition yields a unique weak solution without requiring f(0)=0. With the optimal Poincaré constant it reads ϵ<λ1​.

Contraction iteration error bound (d(xn​,x∗​)≤Lnd(x1​,x0​)/(1−L))

Words: 80
Contraction mapping theorem OurBigBook.com
Successive steps satisfy d(xn+1​,xn​)≤Lnd(x1​,x0​). Summing the remaining steps with the triangle inequality gives a bound available before the iteration starts:
d(xn​,x∗​)≤1−LLn​d(x1​,x0​)(n≥0).
(150)
After computing a new step, the contraction mapping gives the often sharper bound
d(xn​,x∗​)≤1−LL​d(xn​,xn−1​)(n≥1).
(151)
Equivalently, the residual at any z∈X satisfies d(z,x∗​)≤d(z,Tz)/(1−L). These estimates convert visible step sizes into guaranteed distances to an unknown fixed point. When L is close to one, the factor 1/(1−L) can be large: a small step alone needs interpretation through the contraction constant.

Cosine fixed-point iteration (xn+1​=cosxn​)

Words: 264
Contraction mapping theorem OurBigBook.com
Use radians and take T(x)=cosx on the closed interval [0,1]. This is a complete metric space with distance ∣x−y∣, and T([0,1])=[cos1,1]⊂[0,1]. The mean value theorem and ∣T′(x)∣=sinx≤sin1 give a contraction mapping with L=sin1≈0.841471<1. Both the interval and its preservation matter; a small derivative by itself would not ensure that all subsequent approximations stay in the chosen space.
Starting at x0​=0 gives x1​=1, x2​≈0.540302, x3​≈0.857553, and x4​≈0.654290. The cosine is decreasing here, so successive iterates alternate around the unique fixed point x∗​≈0.739085133215161. The contraction iteration error bound needs no prior knowledge of this numerical value. At step 40, x40​≈0.739085078689123 and the latest-step bound is below 7.20×10−7, certifying error below one millionth for exact iteration. The initial-step bound requires 91 iterations for the same tolerance. The observed step-40 error is only about 5.45×10−8; the guarantees allow less favorable behavior than this example actually exhibits.
This is the beauty of the contraction mapping theorem: a uniform local improvement controls the entire infinite process. Completeness is essential. On the incomplete interval (0,1), the contraction mapping T(x)=x/2 keeps every iterate inside but has no fixed point there; its missing limit is zero. Banach's 1922 paper developed abstract methods for different spaces of functions with applications to integral equations, a motivation still visible whenever repeated approximation is used to construct a function.[ref]

Contraction mapping theorem OurBigBook.com
Let A be differentiable on a neighbourhood of a closed radius-r ball in a Banach space, with ∥DA∥≤κ<1 on that ball. If ∥A(p0​)−p0​∥≤(1−κ)r, the mean-value estimate gives A(B)⊆B and ∥A(p)−A(q)∥≤κ∥p−q∥. The contraction mapping theorem supplies exactly one fixed point in B, and its distance from p0​ is at most ∥A(p0​)−p0​∥/(1−κ).

Contraction property of closed subsets characterizes completeness

Words: 53
Contraction mapping theorem OurBigBook.com
A metric space is complete if and only if every contraction mapping of every nonempty closed subset into itself has a fixed point. For the converse, a nonconvergent Cauchy sequence contains a rapidly approaching subsequence whose point set is closed and whose shift is a contraction without a fixed point. Requiring the property only on the whole space is a different, weaker condition.

If the space has two distinct points, changing only the second input coordinate shows that one step preserves some nonzero distance exactly, so it is not itself a strict contraction. Two iterations apply f to both coordinates and therefore contract with the same constant as f. This provides a direct example of a map whose iterate is contractive although the map is not.

A contraction constant for a function T on a metric space is a single q<1 that bounds the ratio d(Tx,Ty)/d(x,y) for every distinct pair. Pointwise strict inequalities d(Tx,Ty)<d(x,y) do not imply such a common constant. For a differentiable function on an interval, the mean value theorem shows that ∣T′∣≤q<1 supplies a contraction constant.
Contraction property under equivalent metrics
Words: 72
Contraction mapping OurBigBook.com
The same self-map can be a contraction mapping for one metric but not for a bilipschitz equivalent metric. On three points with distances d′(x,y)=d′(x,z)=2, d′(y,z)=1, the map f(x)=y, f(y)=f(z)=z has Lipschitz constant 1/2. For the discrete metric, its Lipschitz constant is one. The metrics satisfy d≤d′≤2d, so they preserve topology and completeness but not the strict numerical contraction condition. A contraction mapping theorem fixed-point proof therefore needs the specified metric and its contraction constant.

If a self-map T of a nonempty complete metric space has an iterate Tn that is a contraction mapping, the contraction mapping theorem gives a unique fixed point a of Tn. Indeed, ∥xn+1​−xn​∥≤αn​∥x1​−x0​∥ makes the orbit Cauchy by summing successive increments. The first bound makes T continuous, so the limit is fixed. Since αn​→0, the bounds also imply uniqueness. Root mean square (xrms​=⟨x2⟩​)

Words: 109 Articles: 1
Analysis OurBigBook.com
The root mean square of a real function or data set is the square root of its mean square. A sinusoid of amplitude a has root mean square ∣a∣/2​. For orthogonal or uncorrelated zero-mean components, the squared root mean square of their sum is the sum of their mean squares; this follows by expanding the square and observing that all cross terms average to zero.

The raw root mean square of a random variable is E[X2]​, whereas its r.m.s. fluctuation about its mean is the standard deviation E[(X−μ)2]​. The former cannot be smaller than ∣μ∣. Experimental phrases such as r.m.s. noise or temperature spread usually refer to the latter and should state the reference level.

Half the full width between the two half-height points of a symmetric line profile. Stating whether a Doppler formula uses HWHM or FWHM avoids a factor-of-two resolution error.
